---
title: Anti-patterns
description: "What not to do when building an Arkitekt app, in any language: getter actions, UI state that mirrors the app, large arrays and high-frequency updates in state, device handles in state, work at import time, orchestration in plain actions and large data inline. Each with an example and what to do instead."
type: concept
---

> **With great power comes great responsibility.**

Arkitekt makes a lot of things one line away. Mark a class as state, and every UI and every other
app sees it change live. Take a client by annotation, and your function can reach the whole
platform. Declare an action, and anyone in your organization can call it from a form, a script or a
workflow.

That reach is the point, and it is also how apps go wrong. A value published to the platform is
sent, journaled and pushed to every watcher on each change. A UI panel that keeps its own idea of
the device can be wrong for everyone looking at it. None of the patterns below raises an error.
They work in a demo and break once a second user, a workflow or a restart turns up.

Each one breaks one of [the patterns behind Arkitekt](/docs/build/patterns), which explain why
the rule exists. The examples are Python, the reference client. The patterns apply unchanged to Rust and Kotlin,
because they are about the [shared model](/docs/build/shared-concepts), not the syntax. `Hardware`
in the examples stands for the app's device and model, kept in a context as
[shown below](#handles).

| Anti-pattern | Do this instead |
|---|---|
| [Getter actions for state](#getters) | Publish it with `@app.state` |
| [UI that keeps its own copy of the app's state](#ui-state) | Bind the UI to the published state |
| [Large arrays in state](#large-arrays) | Store the data, publish a reference or a summary |
| [State as a real-time channel](#frequency) | Publish what is actionable at that rate, stream the rest |
| [Device handles and models in state](#handles) | `@app.context` |
| [Work at import time, module-level globals](#import-time) | Startup hooks and context |
| [A plain action that orchestrates](#orchestration) | `@app.workflow` with a protocol |
| [Large data inline in ports](#inline-data) | Structures, passed by reference |
| [Memory structures as the default](#memory-structures) | One action for steps that belong together, or a data service |

## Getter actions for state [#getters]

**Don't.** Offer an action whose only job is to report what the app already knows:

```python
@app.action
def get_position() -> tuple[float, float]:
    """Get Position"""
    return stage.x_um, stage.y_um
```

Every UI that wants to show the position now has to call it over and over. Each call is a task:
scheduled, routed to your agent, run, recorded. Ten open panels polling twice a second are twenty
tasks a second that do nothing. Between two polls the value is unknown, and a workflow cannot
[guard](/docs/build/python/durable-execution#guard) on an action.

**Do.** Publish it as state. Assigning a field sends the change once, to everyone watching:

```python
@app.state
class Stage:
    x_um: float = 0.0
    y_um: float = 0.0
    moving: bool = False


@app.startup
def home() -> Stage:
    return Stage()


@app.action
def move_to(stage: Stage, hardware: Hardware, x_um: float, y_um: float) -> None:
    """Move To"""
    stage.moving = True
    hardware.driver.move(x_um, y_um)
    stage.x_um, stage.y_um = x_um, y_um   # published
    stage.moving = False
```

Actions are for things that **do** something or **compute** something. If the answer is already
sitting in the app, it is state.

## UI that keeps its own copy of the app's state [#ui-state]

**Don't.** Let the panel decide what the device is doing because a button was clicked:

```xml
<Blok kind="agent" context="panel">
  <local name="acquiring" default={false} />
  <Card>
    <Switch bind={acquiring} />
    <Button onClick={self.start()}>Start</Button>
    <Text>{acquiring ? "Acquiring" : "Idle"}</Text>
  </Card>
</Blok>
```

The `acquiring` local is the panel's own opinion. It says "Acquiring" when the call failed, when a
workflow or a colleague stopped the camera, when the agent restarted, and in every other panel
that was not the one clicked. The same mistake exists outside bloks: a Qt widget that flips
`self.running = True` in its click handler, or a web frontend that sets a flag before the request
returns.

**Do.** The app owns the truth and publishes it. The UI only shows it and calls actions:

```xml
<Blok kind="agent" context="panel">
  <Card>
    <Text>{self.Camera.acquiring ? "Acquiring" : "Idle"}</Text>
    <Button onClick={self.start() into starting}
            disabled={self.Camera.acquiring || starting.running}>Start</Button>
    <Button onClick={self.stop()} disabled={!self.Camera.acquiring}>Stop</Button>
  </Card>
</Blok>
```

`self.Camera.acquiring` is the state the app publishes. `into starting` gives the panel the record
of its own call, so it can show that a request is in flight (`starting.running`) without claiming
anything about the device.

The rule cuts both ways. **View state** belongs to the viewer and stays out of `@app.state`: which
tab is open, a slider value before Apply, which row is expanded. That is what a blok's `<local>` is
for. A good test: if two people look at the app at the same time, should they see the same value?
Then it is app state. Could they disagree? Then it is view state.

## Large arrays in state [#large-arrays]

**Don't.** Put the data itself into state because it is convenient to show:

```python
@app.state
class Acquisition:
    frames: int = 0
    histogram: list[float] | None = None          # 65 536 bins
    last_frame: list[list[int]] | None = None     # 2048 x 2048 pixels, as lists
```

A `numpy` array is refused when the app is assembled, so this usually shows up as `.tolist()`.
State is sent as a patch on every change, recorded in the agent's journal, and held by the server
for anyone who asks. A 2048 × 2048 frame as JSON is tens of megabytes, on every update, to every
watcher.

**Do.** Store large data where large data lives, and publish a **reference**, or a **summary** that
fits in a sentence:

```python
from mikro import Mikro
from mikro.arkitekt.specs import Image


@app.state
class Acquisition:
    frames: int = 0
    saturated_pixels: int = 0                     # a summary someone can act on
    last_image: Image | None = None               # a reference: Mikro holds the pixels


@app.action
def snap(acquisition: Acquisition, hardware: Hardware, mikro: Mikro) -> Image:
    """Snap"""
    frame = hardware.camera.snap()
    image = mikro.create_array_dataset(data=frame, ...).lens()
    acquisition.frames += 1
    acquisition.saturated_pixels = int((frame == frame.max()).sum())
    acquisition.last_image = image                # only the id travels
    return image
```

Keep state to what you would write on a whiteboard next to the instrument: positions, flags,
counters, a barcode, a reference. Anything you would need a viewer for goes into a data service.

## State as a real-time channel [#frequency]

This is the one that hurts most, because it looks like it works.

**Don't.** Push to state at the rate things happen:

```python
@app.background
def acquire(camera: Camera, hardware: Hardware) -> None:
    while True:
        frame = hardware.camera.snap()            # 50 frames a second
        camera.frame_number += 1                  # 50 updates a second
        camera.mean_intensity = float(frame.mean())
        camera.stage_z_um = hardware.stage.read_z()   # a 1 kHz encoder, read in the loop
```

State is not a stream. **Every assignment is one update**: its own numbered frame, sent to the
server, recorded in the agent's journal and fanned out to every watcher. Nothing is merged or
dropped, so the loop above sends 150 frames a second, each one stored, and every 60th update also
carries a full snapshot of all the app's states. Those frames share one ordered queue with the
progress, logs and results of the app's tasks, so a chatty state slows down everything else the
agent reports.

And there is **always latency**: every update makes the trip from the agent through the server to
each viewer. A live view built on state lags and stutters, and a control loop built on it reacts
too late. Neither is what state is for.

**Push only state you might want to track during a workflow, and only at a rate someone can act
on.** Two questions decide whether a value belongs in state, and how often to write it:

1. **Would a workflow guard on it, or a person decide on it?** `acquiring`, `exposure_ms`,
   `saturated`, the current plate barcode: yes. A per-frame counter, a running mean, the raw encoder
   value: no.
2. **Is it actionable at the frequency you push it?** A temperature that a workflow waits on is
   actionable once a second. A focus value that changes 50 times a second is not actionable 50
   times a second by anyone watching through a server. Write it when it *changes meaningfully*
   (settled, out of range, crossed a threshold), not every time you read it.

**Do.** Publish the few actionable facts, at their own pace, and send the live data through a
channel built for it. For video and fast signals that is Lovekit (the `lovekit` extra), which
streams over WebRTC. State only carries *which* streams exist:

```python
from lovekit import Lovekit, VideoStream, to_rgba
from lovekit.api.schema import Stream


@app.state
class Camera:
    exposure_ms: float = 10.0
    acquiring: bool = False
    saturated: bool = False                       # changes rarely, and a workflow can guard on it
    streams: list[Stream] | None = None           # where to watch, not what to watch


@app.background
async def live_view(camera: Camera, hardware: Hardware, lovekit: Lovekit) -> None:
    async with lovekit.publish([VideoStream("camera", title="Live view")]) as live:
        camera.streams = list(live.streams)       # published once
        while True:
            frame = await hardware.camera.asnap()
            await live.video("camera").send(to_rgba(frame))   # 50 fps, never touches state
            saturated = bool((frame == 65535).any())
            if saturated != camera.saturated:     # publish the change, not the reading
                camera.saturated = saturated
```

The same split holds for data that is not video: a `DataStream` for a spectrum or a trace you want
to watch live, and a `@app.state` field for the one number a workflow decides on.

When several fields change together, make them **one** update, so nobody sees the stage at the new
x and the old y, and the platform gets one frame instead of three:

```python
with task.updating(stage):
    stage.x_um, stage.y_um = x_um, y_um
    stage.moving = False
```

## Device handles and models in state [#handles]

**Don't.** Make the open device or the loaded network a state field so that every action can reach
it:

```python
@app.state
class Microscope:
    driver: object                               # a serial port, a DLL handle
    model: object                                # 2 GB of weights
```

State is published, so its fields have to be serialized and sent. A handle cannot be, and a model
should not be.

**Do.** Put private, process-bound objects in a **context**: shared by the app's actions, built by a
startup hook, never published.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass


@app.context
@dataclass
class Hardware:
    driver: Driver
    model: Network


@app.startup
def open_hardware() -> Hardware:
    return Hardware(driver=Driver("/dev/ttyUSB0"), model=load("model.pt"))


@app.shutdown
def close_hardware(hardware: Hardware) -> None:
    hardware.driver.close()
```

Publish what the device *is doing* as state. Keep what the device *is* as context.

## Work at import time, module-level globals [#import-time]

**Don't.** Open the device or load the model when the module is imported, and keep it in a global:

```python
driver = Driver("/dev/ttyUSB0")                  # runs on import
model = load("model.pt")

@app.action
def segment(image: Image) -> LabelMask:
    """Segment"""
    return model.predict(image)
```

The CLI imports your module to inspect, check and package it, and `arkitekt run dev` imports it
again on every reload. Each import opens the port and loads the weights, on the build machine and
in CI. A global is also invisible to the platform: nobody can see it, lock it or test with a
stand-in.

**Do.** Do the work in a startup hook and take the result by annotation, as in the context example
above. Tests can then call the action with a fake context, and `arkitekt inspect variables` stays
quiet.

## A plain action that orchestrates [#orchestration]

**Don't.** Call other actions from inside an `@app.action`, or drive a multi-step experiment from a
loop in a script:

```python
from rekuest.client.client import RekuestCaller


@app.action
def stain_and_measure(well: str, rekuest: RekuestCaller) -> float:
    """Stain And Measure"""
    cells = rekuest.call(COUNT_CELLS, well=well)    # refused: RootOnlyCallError
    rekuest.call(DISPENSE, well=well, volume_ul=0.5 * cells)
    return rekuest.call(READ, well=well)
```

A plain action whose agent dies leaves no trace of which calls it made. Did the dispense happen?
Nobody can say, so nothing can be resumed. Arkitekt refuses this: a client call from inside a task
raises `RootOnlyCallError`, and a plain action that depends on an action demand is reported when
the app is assembled.

**Do.** Declare what you need as a protocol and orchestrate in an `@app.workflow`. Its calls are
recorded, so a crashed workflow is resumed where it was:

```python
@app.declare(app="liquid-handler", auto_resolvable=True, min=1)
class LiquidHandler(Protocol):
    def dispense(self, well: str, volume_ul: float) -> None:
        """Dispense"""
        ...


@app.workflow
def stain_and_measure(well: str, handler: LiquidHandler, *, task: Task) -> None:
    """Stain And Measure"""
    handler.dispense(well=well, volume_ul=0.5)
```

See [Workflows](/docs/build/python/workflows) and [Durable execution](/docs/build/durable-execution).

## Large data inline in ports [#inline-data]

**Don't.** Pass pixels, traces or tables as plain values between actions:

```python
@app.action
def denoise(pixels: list[list[float]]) -> list[list[float]]:
    """Denoise"""
    ...
```

The arguments are serialized into the task, stored with its history and sent through the server on
every call. The form in Orkestrator cannot offer "an image" to pick, the workflow editor cannot
check that the output fits the next step, and provenance has no dataset to point at.

**Do.** Take and return a **structure**. The data stays in its service and only a reference travels:

```python
from mikro.arkitekt.specs import Volume


@app.action
def denoise(volume: Volume, mikro: Mikro) -> Volume:
    """Denoise"""
    ...
```

For arrays that only move between actions of one app, a
[memory structure](/docs/build/python/types#in-memory-structures) keeps them on the agent without
storing them anywhere. Use that sparingly, for the reasons in the next section.

## Memory structures as the default [#memory-structures]

**Don't.** Register `np.ndarray` as a memory structure and split every pipeline into small actions
that hand arrays to each other:

```python
app.memory_structure(np.ndarray)


@app.action
def read(path: str) -> np.ndarray: ...

@app.action
def smooth(image: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

@app.action
def segment(image: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray: ...

@app.action
def count(labels: np.ndarray) -> int: ...
```

It looks clean, and it quietly makes the app **stateful**. Every array an action returns stays in
the agent's memory after its task has ended. It is not dropped when the next action has used it:
the agent keeps it until Rekuest tells it to collect that reference, or until the agent stops. Run
this pipeline on every new acquisition, and the agent holds three arrays per run, growing until
the process is killed. Meanwhile every reference works only on that one agent: a second agent of the
same app cannot resolve it, and a restart breaks every reference a running workflow still holds.

**Do.** Keep steps that always run together in **one** action. Nothing is kept, nothing is
referenced, and the arrays are freed when the task ends:

```python
@app.action
def count_cells(path: str, sigma: float = 2.0) -> int:
    """Count Cells"""
    image = tifffile.imread(path)
    labels = segment(gaussian(image, sigma))      # plain functions, not actions
    return int(labels.max())
```

When an intermediate result is worth looking at, keeping or passing to another app, store it in a
data service and pass the reference. A memory structure is for the narrow case of an interactive
pipeline on one agent, where a person rewires the steps, on an app that restarts often enough that
its memory stays bounded. See
[Arrays between actions](/docs/build/python/examples/in-memory#use-it-sparingly).

## A checklist

- [ ] Nothing is a getter: values the app knows are `@app.state`.
- [ ] UIs bind to the app's state, and keep only view state (`<local>`) of their own.
- [ ] State holds no arrays: references and summaries only.
- [ ] Every state field is something a workflow could guard on or a person could act on, and it is
      written when it changes meaningfully, not on every reading.
- [ ] Live video and fast signals go through Lovekit streams, not state.
- [ ] Handles and models are `@app.context`, built in `@app.startup`.
- [ ] Importing the module does nothing but declare.
- [ ] Anything that calls other actions is an `@app.workflow`.
- [ ] Images, traces and tables cross action boundaries as structures.
- [ ] Memory structures are the exception: steps that belong together are one action.
